analysis.one_liner: Requires groups spending money in elections to disclose their big donors and tightens the ban on foreign money.
analysis.headline: A campaign-transparency bill backed by 211 of 231 House Democrats never got a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would have required any corporation, union, Super PAC, or tax-exempt group that spends money on elections to reveal everyone who gave it $10,000 or more, and to name its top funders right on its political ads. It would also have tightened the ban on foreign money in elections, extending it to online and digital ads and to ballot initiatives, and required an annual federal audit of illicit foreign money in campaigns. The bill was referred to two House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters. Today, groups can spend unlimited amounts on political ads without saying where the money came from. This bill would have let anyone see which donors of $10,000 or more were behind a group's election spending, see the top five funders listed on the ads themselves, and know that corporate executives had certified no foreign money was involved in the decision. Ordinary citizens trying to judge a political ad would have been able to follow the money behind it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to follow the money

how_it_helps.text: Any corporation, labor organization, Super PAC, or tax-exempt group spending more than $10,000 on election-related ads would have to file a sworn statement naming every person who gave it $10,000 or more during the cycle, along with each disbursement over $1,000.
Corporations and other entities would have to disclose their beneficial owners — the real people who control or profit from them — so donors could not hide behind shell entities.

Political ads would have to carry a 'Stand By Every Ad' statement, like the 'I'm so-and-so and I approve this message' tag on candidate ads, and list the organization's top five funders (or top two for radio), so viewers could see who was paying for the ad.

The ban on foreign money in elections would be extended to paid internet and digital ads, to State and local ballot initiatives, and to foreign nationals participating in spending decisions; corporate CEOs would have to certify under penalty of perjury that no foreign national directed their election spending.
The Federal Election Commission would have to audit each federal election cycle for illicit foreign money and report its findings and recommendations to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the groups that spend money in politics: corporations, unions, Super PACs, and tax-exempt nonprofit organizations would bear the paperwork and compliance burden of donor disclosure, beneficial-owner reporting, and expanded ad disclaimers. More fundamentally, wealthy donors and companies that currently fund election ads anonymously would lose that anonymity. Nonprofit advocacy groups and trade associations could no longer run 'issue ads' without revealing their large funders.

drawbacks.text: Disclosure imposes real compliance costs: covered groups would have to track and report every $10,000+ donor and every $1,000+ disbursement within 24 hours of crossing the spending threshold, a burden that falls hardest on small advocacy organizations and charities-adjacent groups even though the bill exempts ordinary commercial receipts.

Publicly naming donors can expose private citizens to harassment or retaliation; the bill responds with an exception for people facing serious threats, harassment, or reprisals, and allows donors to forbid use of their money for politics, but critics of donor disclosure argue these protections do not remove the chilling effect on political giving.

The foreign-money provisions put a new legal duty on individual corporate executives, who would have to personally certify under penalty of perjury each year that no foreign national participated in their company's political spending decisions — a certification that may be hard to make with confidence in large multinationals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is modest: paperwork for political spenders against voters' ability to see who funds the ads aimed at them. The compliance burden is genuine, especially for smaller nonprofits, and the threat-harassment exception is only a partial answer to donor-privacy concerns. But the bill's centerpiece — naming $10,000+ donors and putting top funders on the ads themselves — targets the largest sums, not small givers, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly cited disclosure as the least restrictive way to regulate election spending. On balance the benefits to voters outweigh the compliance costs; the bill's failure was about who held power, not about a flaw in the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Administration and Ways and Means committees, neither of which ever took it up, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Cicilline introduced the bill on May 23, 2019, and it was referred to the Committee on House Administration and, for provisions in its jurisdiction, to the Ways and Means Committee.
Within days, 211 of the 231 House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors — more than nine in ten of the party's members — while no Republican did.
No committee ever held a markup or voted the bill out, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the record shows no action of any kind after the initial referral.
The bill died with the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies, wealthy donors, and tax-exempt groups that fund election ads anonymously are better off: because the bill never advanced, they kept the ability to spend without naming their big donors, and no foreign-money audit of election spending was created.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DISCLOSE Act of 2019 on May 23, 2019.

for.name: 211 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, more than nine in ten of the party's House members.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill; it stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions within its jurisdiction.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsor and opposed campaign-finance disclosure legislation of this kind throughout the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote, prioritizing the broader H.R. 1 democracy package, which passed the House in March 2019 and contained its own DISCLOSE provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely one-sided: 211 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored the bill and not a single one of the 197 House Republicans did, and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Corporate political spenders and 'dark money' nonprofits (501(c)(4) and 501(c)(6) groups)
industries.note: These groups exist to influence elections and policy while keeping their funders confidential; the bill would have forced them to name every donor of $10,000 or more and disclose beneficial owners, ending the anonymity that makes their spending model work.
Groups accepting unlimited donations would face 24-hour disclosure of their $10,000+ donors and transfers used for campaign spending, shrinking the pool of donors willing to fund them.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill and would face the same donor and disbursement reporting, though member dues were treated as ordinary receipts and unions generally disclose more already than anonymously-funded corporate-aligned groups.

industries.industry: Broadcast, cable, and digital advertising platforms
industries.note: New disclaimer and top-funder requirements would apply to online and broadcast political ads, creating compliance work, but the rules also extended the foreign-money ban to paid digital ads, a market where such rules barely existed.
